questions.stem: A particle undergoes a displacement $\vec{s}_1 = -15\text{ m}\;\hat{i}$ followed by $\vec{s}_2 = +15\text{ m}\;\hat{i}$. Which statement fundamentally characterizes the physical state of the particle upon completion of $\vec{s}_2$?

options.B: The two displacements cancel dynamically, meaning no physical distance was traversed.

D.diagnostic: Misunderstands coordinate signs, believing negative vectors destroy the reference frame.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A student claims that if two vectors satisfy $\vec{A} + \vec{B} = \vec{0}$, then their dot product $\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B}$ must be strictly non-positive, and their magnitudes must be equal. Is this claim mathematically and physically justified?

options.B: Unjustified: two vectors can sum to zero with different magnitudes if one has negative mass.
options.C: Partially justified: magnitudes are equal, but the dot product is always zero because the vectors cancel.
options.D: Unjustified: $\vec{A} + \vec{B} = \vec{0}$ implies $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ must both be the null vector $\vec{0}$.

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Deduce opposite vector magnitude equality and non-positive scalar product invariant.

A.diagnostic: Correct. $\vec{A} + \vec{B} = \vec{0} \implies \vec{B} = -\vec{A}$. Hence $|\vec{B}| = |-\vec{A}| = |\vec{A}|$, and $\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} = \vec{A} \cdot (-\vec{A}) = -|\vec{A}|^2 \le 0$ (strictly negative unless both are null).

B.diagnostic: Invents unphysical negative mass concept; vector norms are strictly non-negative.

C.diagnostic: Confuses vector sum cancellation with scalar product, which measures parallel projection.

D.diagnostic: Assumes only the trivial solution exists, ignoring all non-zero antiparallel pairs.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: If $\vec{A} + \vec{B} = \vec{0}$, what is the algebraic relation between $\vec{B}$ and $\vec{A}$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Subtracting $\vec{A}$ yields $\vec{B} = -\vec{A}$; $\vec{B}$ is the additive inverse (opposite vector) of $\vec{A}$.

progressive_hints.title: Geometric Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: How does the magnitude $|-\vec{A}|$ compare to $|\vec{A}|$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: By definition of vector norm, $|-\vec{A}| = |-1|\,|\vec{A}| = |\vec{A}|$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Substitute $\vec{B} = -\vec{A}$ into the dot product $\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B}$. What is the result?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} = \vec{A} \cdot (-\vec{A}) = -(\vec{A} \cdot \vec{A}) = -|\vec{A}|^2$, which is strictly $\le 0$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: \vec{A} + \vec{B} = \vec{0} \implies \vec{B} = -\vec{A} - Additive inverse in vector space.
reasoning_ladder.represent: |\vec{B}| = |-\vec{A}| = |\vec{A}| - Opposite vectors have identical length and reversed orientation.
reasoning_ladder.connect: \vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} = |\vec{A}||\vec{B}| \cos(180^\circ) = -|\vec{A}||\vec{A}| = -|\vec{A}|^2 - Angle between a vector and its opposite is exactly 180 degrees.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: -|\vec{A}|^2 \le 0 \text{ for all } \vec{A} \in \mathbb{R}^n - The square of any real magnitude is non-negative, so its negation is non-positive.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: \text{The claim is fully justified: } |\vec{A}| = |\vec{B}| \text{ and } \vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} \le 0. - Rigorous algebraic and geometric consistency demonstrated.

derivation_steps: Step 1 (Understand the physical regime): \vec{A} + \vec{B} = \vec{0} \implies \vec{B} = -\vec{A} [Additive inverse in vector space.]
Step 2 (Represent the physical configuration): |\vec{B}| = |-\vec{A}| = |\vec{A}| [Opposite vectors have identical length and reversed orientation.]

Step 3 (Connect governing physical laws): \vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} = |\vec{A}||\vec{B}| \cos(180^\circ) = -|\vec{A}||\vec{A}| = -|\vec{A}|^2 [Angle between a vector and its opposite is exactly 180 degrees.]
Step 4 (Calculate & execute formal derivation): -|\vec{A}|^2 \le 0 \text{ for all } \vec{A} \in \mathbb{R}^n [The square of any real magnitude is non-negative, so its negation is non-positive.]

Step 5 (Interpret the physical outcome): \text{The claim is fully justified: } |\vec{A}| = |\vec{B}| \text{ and } \vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} \le 0. [Rigorous algebraic and geometric consistency demonstrated.]

progressive_hints.prompt_question: In which Cartesian quadrant does 'North of West' point?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: West corresponds to negative $x$ and North to positive $y$; hence the vector lies in Quadrant II ($x < 0, y > 0$).

progressive_hints.title: Geometric Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Which axis is adjacent to the specified $40.0^\circ$ angle?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: 'North of West' measures $40.0^\circ$ away from the West axis; the adjacent component is along the West ($-x$) axis.

progressive_hints.prompt_question: How do trigonometric definitions translate into signed components?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $d_x = -|\vec{d}| \cos 40.0^\circ$ and $d_y = +|\vec{d}| \sin 40.0^\circ$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: \text{Vector in Quadrant II with reference angle } 40^\circ \text{ from negative } x\text{-axis}. - Compass specification 'North of West' establishes base axis as West.
reasoning_ladder.represent: \vec{d} = d_x \hat{i} + d_y \hat{j},\quad d_x < 0,\quad d_y > 0 - Quadrant II Cartesian sign signature.

Step 3 (Connect governing physical laws): d_x = -|\vec{d}| \cos\theta,\quad d_y = +|\vec{d}| \sin\theta [Standard right-triangle projection onto adjacent and opposite axes.]
Step 4 (Calculate & execute formal derivation): d_x = -12.0 \times 0.7660 = -9.19\text{ m};\quad d_y = +12.0 \times 0.6428 = +7.71\text{ m} [Direct numerical computation.]

reasoning_ladder.interpret: \vec{R} = 15.0\text{ m at } 53.1^\circ\text{ North of East}. - Straight-line displacement is strictly shorter than 21 m path distance.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: An autonomous drone flies $4.0\text{ km}$ due East, then $3.0\text{ km}$ due North. It then executes a third displacement $\vec{d}_3$ that returns it exactly to its initial launching pad. What is the magnitude and directional heading of $\vec{d}_3$?

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Model closed vector polygon equilibrium condition and invert net displacement.

A.diagnostic: Correct. Return to origin requires closed polygon $\vec{d}_1 + \vec{d}_2 + \vec{d}_3 = \vec{0} \implies \vec{d}_3 = -(\vec{d}_1 + \vec{d}_2) = -4\hat{i} - 3\hat{j}$. Magnitude is $\sqrt{(-4)^2 + (-3)^2} = 5.0\text{ km}$, angle is $\arctan(3/4) \approx 36.9^\circ$ South of West.

B.diagnostic: Provides the net forward displacement $\vec{d}_1 + \vec{d}_2$ instead of the return vector $\vec{d}_3$.

C.diagnostic: Adds scalar legs $4 + 3 = 7\text{ km}$.

D.diagnostic: Subtracts scalar legs $4 - 3 = 1\text{ km}$.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What does 'returns exactly to the start' mean for the vector sum of all three displacements?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: A closed loop means the total resultant displacement is the null vector: $\vec{d}_1 + \vec{d}_2 + \vec{d}_3 = \vec{0}$.

progressive_hints.title: Geometric Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: How is $\vec{d}_3$ related algebraically to $\vec{d}_1 + \vec{d}_2$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $\vec{d}_3 = -(\vec{d}_1 + \vec{d}_2)$. It is the exact opposite of the net displacement of the first two legs.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What are the components of $\vec{d}_3$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $d_{3x} = -4.0\text{ km}$ (West) and $d_{3y} = -3.0\text{ km}$ (South). Magnitude is $\sqrt{(-4)^2 + (-3)^2} = 5.0\text{ km}$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: \sum_{i=1}^3 \vec{d}_i = \vec{0} \implies \text{Closed triangle in Euclidean plane.} - Returning to start forms a closed vector polygon.
reasoning_ladder.represent: \vec{d}_1 = 4.0\,\hat{i},\quad \vec{d}_2 = 3.0\,\hat{j},\quad \vec{d}_3 = d_{3x}\,\hat{i} + d_{3y}\,\hat{j} - Orthogonal basis representation.
reasoning_ladder.connect: \vec{d}_3 = -(\vec{d}_1 + \vec{d}_2) = -4.0\,\hat{i} - 3.0\,\hat{j} - Additive inverse closure condition.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: |\vec{d}_3| = \sqrt{(-4.0)^2 + (-3.0)^2} = \sqrt{16 + 9} = 5.0\text{ km};\quad \tan\theta = \frac{-3.0}{-4.0} = 0.75 \implies 36.87^\circ\text{ S of W} - Component evaluation in Quadrant III.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: \vec{d}_3 \text{ points directly back to the origin with magnitude } 5.0\text{ km}. - Validates polygon closure identity.

derivation_steps: Step 1 (Understand the physical regime): \sum_{i=1}^3 \vec{d}_i = \vec{0} \implies \text{Closed triangle in Euclidean plane.} [Returning to start forms a closed vector polygon.]
Step 2 (Represent the physical configuration): \vec{d}_1 = 4.0\,\hat{i},\quad \vec{d}_2 = 3.0\,\hat{j},\quad \vec{d}_3 = d_{3x}\,\hat{i} + d_{3y}\,\hat{j} [Orthogonal basis representation.]
Step 3 (Connect governing physical laws): \vec{d}_3 = -(\vec{d}_1 + \vec{d}_2) = -4.0\,\hat{i} - 3.0\,\hat{j} [Additive inverse closure condition.]

Step 4 (Calculate & execute formal derivation): |\vec{d}_3| = \sqrt{(-4.0)^2 + (-3.0)^2} = \sqrt{16 + 9} = 5.0\text{ km};\quad \tan\theta = \frac{-3.0}{-4.0} = 0.75 \implies 36.87^\circ\text{ S of W} [Component evaluation in Quadrant III.]
Step 5 (Interpret the physical outcome): \vec{d}_3 \text{ points directly back to the origin with magnitude } 5.0\text{ km}. [Validates polygon closure identity.]

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: An object's velocity changes from $\vec{v}_i = (4.0, 0.0)\text{ m/s}$ to $\vec{v}_f = (0.0, 4.0)\text{ m/s}$. Which component expression correctly represents the change vector $\Delta\vec{v}$, and what angle does it form relative to the positive $x$-axis?

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Execute component-wise vector subtraction and determine Quadrant II polar direction.

A.diagnostic: Correct. $\Delta\vec{v} = \vec{v}_f - \vec{v}_i = (0 - 4, 4 - 0) = (-4.0, 4.0)\text{ m/s}$. In Quadrant II, angle is $180^\circ - 45^\circ = 135.0^\circ$.

B.diagnostic: Adds vectors instead of subtracting: $(0+4, 4+0) = (4, 4)$.

C.diagnostic: Calculates $\vec{v}_i - \vec{v}_f = (4, -4)$ instead of final minus initial.

D.diagnostic: Applies negative sign to both components indiscriminately.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the universal definition of a change vector $\Delta\vec{X}$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: A change vector is always defined as final minus initial: $\Delta\vec{X} = \vec{X}_{\text{final}} - \vec{X}_{\text{initial}}$.

progressive_hints.title: Geometric Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: How do you evaluate component-by-component subtraction?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $\Delta v_x = v_{fx} - v_{ix} = 0.0 - 4.0 = -4.0\text{ m/s}$, and $\Delta v_y = v_{fy} - v_{iy} = 4.0 - 0.0 = +4.0\text{ m/s}$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What angle does $(-4.0, +4.0)$ make with the positive $x$-axis?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: It lies in Quadrant II with equal magnitude legs, so $\theta = 180^\circ - 45^\circ = 135.0^\circ$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: \Delta\vec{v} = \vec{v}_f - \vec{v}_i - Definition of physical change vector.
reasoning_ladder.represent: \vec{v}_i = (4.0, 0.0),\quad \vec{v}_f = (0.0, 4.0) - Input state vectors in Cartesian coordinate representation.
reasoning_ladder.connect: \Delta\vec{v} = (v_{fx} - v_{ix})\,\hat{i} + (v_{fy} - v_{iy})\,\hat{j} - Component-wise linear vector operation.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: \Delta\vec{v} = (0.0 - 4.0)\,\hat{i} + (4.0 - 0.0)\,\hat{j} = -4.0\,\hat{i} + 4.0\,\hat{j};\quad \theta = 180^\circ - \arctan(4/4) = 135^\circ - Exact Quadrant II angle determination.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: \Delta\vec{v} = (-4.0, 4.0)\text{ m/s at } 135.0^\circ. - The impulse required to stop horizontal motion and initiate vertical motion points up and back.

questions.stem: A stone whirled on a string moves clockwise in a horizontal circle. At the instant the stone reaches the northernmost point of the circle (12 o'clock position), the string suddenly snaps. Under Newton's first law of motion, in what direction does the stone travel immediately after the break (neglecting air resistance)?

options.B: Radially outward due North, pushed by centrifugal force.
options.C: In a spiraling curved arc outward that gradually straightens out.
options.D: Radially inward toward the center of the circle before falling.

B.diagnostic: Believes a real outward force flings the body radially away from the center.

C.diagnostic: Believes an object retains a 'memory of curvature' after forces vanish, contradicting Newton I.

questions.stem: A textbook rests motionless on a horizontal wooden table. Two vertical forces act: the Earth's downward gravity on the book $\vec{F}_{g}$ and the upward normal contact force of the table on the book $\vec{N}$. Why do $\vec{F}_{g}$ and $\vec{N}$ NOT constitute a Newton's third law action-reaction pair?

options.B: Their magnitudes are not strictly equal if the table surface has friction.
options.C: Action-reaction pairs only apply to moving objects, whereas the book is in static equilibrium.
options.D: The normal force is a reactive fictitious force that does not obey vector algebra.

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Differentiate equilibrium resultant balance from mutual Newton-III dual-body interaction.

A.diagnostic: Correct. Newton's Third Law requires interaction pairs to act on two different mutually interacting bodies ($ec{F}_{A\text{ on }B} = -\vec{F}_{B\text{ on }A}$) and arise from the same fundamental interaction. $ec{F}_g$ and $ec{N}$ both act on the book; their equality $ec{N} + ec{F}_g = ec{0}$ is a Newton's First Law equilibrium consequence, not an action-reaction identity.

B.diagnostic: Friction is horizontal and irrelevant to vertical equilibrium on a level table.

C.diagnostic: Falsely restricts Newton's third law to dynamic systems.

D.diagnostic: Labels normal force as fictitious, confusing macroscopic contact repulsion with non-inertial pseudo forces.

progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the single most critical structural criterion of a Newton-III interaction pair?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: A Newton's third law pair must act on two *different* bodies: $\vec{F}_{12} = -\vec{F}_{21}$ (body 1 on body 2, and body 2 on body 1).

progressive_hints.title: Geometric Representation

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the actual Newton-III reaction partner to the table's upward normal push on the book?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: The reaction partner is the downward contact force exerted by the book on the table ($ec{N}_{\text{book on table}}$).

reasoning_ladder.represent: \text{On book: } \sum \vec{F} = \vec{N}_{\text{table on book}} + \vec{F}_{g,\text{Earth on book}} = \vec{0} - Newton's First Law condition for zero acceleration.

reasoning_ladder.calculate: \vec{N}_{\text{table on book}} = -\vec{N}_{\text{book on table}};\quad \vec{F}_{g,\text{Earth on book}} = -\vec{F}_{g,\text{book on Earth}} - Identification of true third-law reaction partners.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: \vec{N} \text{ and } \vec{F}_g \text{ act on the same body, so they cannot form a Newton-III pair.} - Resolves classical textbook physics misconception.

questions.stem: Two coplanar vectors $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$, each having an identical magnitude of $5.0\text{ units}$, act concurrently at right angles to one another ($\theta = 90.0^\circ$). If the angle between them is now continuously decreased toward $0.0^\circ$, between what theoretical bounds does the resultant magnitude $|ec{A} + \vec{B}|$ vary, and what is its exact value at $\theta = 90.0^\circ$?

options.A: At $\theta = 90.0^\circ$: $|ec{R}| = 5\sqrt{2} \approx 7.07\text{ units}$; Bounds: $[0.0, 10.0]\text{ units}$ as $\theta$ ranges from $180^\circ$ to $0^\circ$.

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Synthesize parallelogram resultant invariant across continuous angle bounds.

A.diagnostic: Correct. By the law of cosines for vectors: $R = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + 2AB\cos\theta}$. At $90^\circ$, $R = \sqrt{25 + 25 + 0} = 5\sqrt{2} \approx 7.07\text{ units}$. The extreme triangle inequality bounds for two 5-unit vectors are $|A - B| = 0$ (at $180^\circ$) and $A + B = 10$ (at $0^\circ$).

B.diagnostic: Assumes orthogonal vectors add linearly like collinear vectors ($5 + 5 = 10$).

C.diagnostic: Assumes resultant equals leg magnitude ($5$).

D.diagnostic: Reports sum of squares $25 + 25$ without taking square root.

progressive_hints.prompt_question: What formula governs the magnitude of the sum of two vectors of magnitude $A$ and $B$ separated by angle $\theta$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: The parallelogram law yields $R = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + 2AB\cos\theta}$.

progressive_hints.title: Geometric Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What does this formula give when $\theta = 90.0^\circ$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Since $\cos(90^\circ) = 0$, $R = \sqrt{5.0^2 + 5.0^2} = \sqrt{50.0} = 5\sqrt{2} \approx 7.07\text{ units}$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What are the minimum and maximum possible values of $R$ for two 5-unit vectors?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Minimum occurs when antiparallel ($\theta = 180^\circ$): $5 - 5 = 0$. Maximum occurs when parallel ($\theta = 0^\circ$): $5 + 5 = 10$. The resultant is strictly bounded by $[0, 10]$.

reasoning_ladder.represent: A = 5.0,\quad B = 5.0,\quad \theta = 90.0^\circ - Equal magnitude orthogonal vector state.
reasoning_ladder.connect: |A - B| \le R \le A + B - Triangle inequality in normed vector spaces.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: R(90^\circ) = \sqrt{5^2 + 5^2 + 2(5)(5)(0)} = \sqrt{50} = 5\sqrt{2} \approx 7.071;\quad R_{\min} = 0,\quad R_{\max} = 10 - Evaluation at orthogonal and extreme collinear angles.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: R = 7.07\text{ units},\quad \text{Bounds: } [0, 10]\text{ units}. - Confirms vector resultant is bounded by triangle inequality.

Step 5 (Interpret the physical outcome): R = 7.07\text{ units},\quad \text{Bounds: } [0, 10]\text{ units}. [Confirms vector resultant is bounded by triangle inequality.]

Declaring East as the positive direction, what is the vector change in momentum $\Delta\vec{p} = m\vec{v}_f - m\vec{v}_i$, and what magnitude of impulse did the wall impart?

progressive_hints.prompt_question: Multiply by mass $m = 0.50\text{ kg}$ to get momentum change and impulse.

Step 4 (Calculate & execute formal derivation): \Delta\vec{p} = 0.50(-6.0 - 8.0)\,\hat{i} = 0.50(-14.0)\,\hat{i} = -7.0\,\hat{i}\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s};\quad |\vec{J}| = 7.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{s} [Direct arithmetic computation.]

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: At an instantaneous point along its curved planar trajectory, a projectile's velocity components are measured as $v_x = 6.0\text{ m/s}$ and $v_y = 8.0\text{ m/s}$. To specify its complete instantaneous velocity state as a foundational bridge into 2D kinematics, which complete vector statement is required?

options.A: Speed = $10.0\text{ m/s}$, directed at $\theta = 53.1^\circ$ above the positive $x$-axis (or $\vec{v} = 6.0\,\hat{i} + 8.0\,\hat{j}\text{ m/s}$)
options.C: Speed = $10.0\text{ m/s}$, directed at $\theta = 36.9^\circ$ above the positive $x$-axis
options.D: Velocity = $10.0\text{ m/s}$ (magnitude alone completely specifies the vector state)

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Synthesize 2D velocity vector state from orthogonal components as planar kinematics bridge.

A.diagnostic: Correct. Speed is scalar magnitude $|\vec{v}| = \sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = 10.0\text{ m/s}$. Direction is angle $\theta = \arctan(v_y / v_x) = \arctan(8/6) \approx 53.13^\circ$ above horizontal. Both magnitude and direction (or full Cartesian components) are strictly mandatory to define the velocity vector.

B.diagnostic: Adds scalar components $6 + 8 = 14\text{ m/s}$.

C.diagnostic: Computes $\arctan(6/8) = 36.9^\circ$, which is angle with the vertical, not horizontal.

D.diagnostic: Claims magnitude alone is sufficient, omitting required directional orientation.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: How is scalar speed related to velocity components $v_x$ and $v_y$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Speed is the Euclidean norm of the velocity vector: $v = |\vec{v}| = \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2} = \sqrt{6.0^2 + 8.0^2} = 10.0\text{ m/s}$.

progressive_hints.title: Geometric Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Why is speed alone insufficient to specify the velocity of the projectile?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Velocity is a physical vector. A complete specification requires both magnitude (speed) and spatial direction (angle relative to a declared axis).

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What angle does the velocity make with the horizontal $+x$-axis?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $\tan\theta = \frac{v_y}{v_x} = \frac{8.0}{6.0} = \frac{4}{3} \implies \theta = \arctan(4/3) \approx 53.1^\circ$ above horizontal.

reasoning_ladder.understand: \vec{v} = v_x \hat{i} + v_y \hat{j} \implies \text{Full state representation in 2D kinematics.} - Bridge from 1D components to 2D planar vector dynamics.
reasoning_ladder.represent: v_x = 6.0\text{ m/s},\quad v_y = 8.0\text{ m/s} - Orthogonal Cartesian coordinates.
reasoning_ladder.connect: |\vec{v}| = \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2},\quad \theta = \arctan\left(\frac{v_y}{v_x}\right) - Conversion from rectangular to polar vector coordinates.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: |\vec{v}| = \sqrt{36.0 + 64.0} = 10.0\text{ m/s};\quad \theta = \arctan(8.0/6.0) = 53.13^\circ - Standard Pythagorean 6-8-10 integer triangle.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: \vec{v} = (10.0\text{ m/s}, 53.1^\circ\text{ above }+x) \equiv 6.0\,\hat{i} + 8.0\,\hat{j}\text{ m/s}. - Establishes necessary condition for 2D trajectory simulation.

derivation_steps: Step 1 (Understand the physical regime): \vec{v} = v_x \hat{i} + v_y \hat{j} \implies \text{Full state representation in 2D kinematics.} [Bridge from 1D components to 2D planar vector dynamics.]
Step 2 (Represent the physical configuration): v_x = 6.0\text{ m/s},\quad v_y = 8.0\text{ m/s} [Orthogonal Cartesian coordinates.]
Step 3 (Connect governing physical laws): |\vec{v}| = \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2},\quad \theta = \arctan\left(\frac{v_y}{v_x}\right) [Conversion from rectangular to polar vector coordinates.]
Step 4 (Calculate & execute formal derivation): |\vec{v}| = \sqrt{36.0 + 64.0} = 10.0\text{ m/s};\quad \theta = \arctan(8.0/6.0) = 53.13^\circ [Standard Pythagorean 6-8-10 integer triangle.]

Step 5 (Interpret the physical outcome): \vec{v} = (10.0\text{ m/s}, 53.1^\circ\text{ above }+x) \equiv 6.0\,\hat{i} + 8.0\,\hat{j}\text{ m/s}. [Establishes necessary condition for 2D trajectory simulation.]

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: An artificial satellite of mass $m$ moves in a circular orbit of radius $r$ around Earth at constant speed $v$. A student asserts that although a massive gravitational force acts continuously on the satellite, the net work done by gravity over any arbitrary orbital arc is strictly zero. Which rigorous vector justification validates this assertion?

options.A: At every instant along the orbit, the gravitational force is radial ($\vec{F}_g \perp d\vec{s}$), making $\cos(90^\circ) = 0$ in the differential work $dW = \vec{F}_g \cdot d\vec{s} = 0$.
options.B: The work is zero because Earth is in a vacuum where no frictional energy can be created.
options.C: Gravity only does work when an object moves in a straight vertical line.
options.D: Work is non-zero over a quarter orbit, but cancels to zero only over a complete $360^\circ$ revolution.

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Justify point-wise vanishing work differential from continuous radial-tangential orthogonality.

A.diagnostic: Correct. In a circular orbit, the instantaneous displacement $d\vec{s}$ is tangential, while the gravitational force $\vec{F}_g$ is strictly radial. Because radial and tangential unit vectors are orthogonal everywhere ($\vec{F}_g \cdot d\vec{s} = F_g ds \cos 90^\circ = 0$), the instantaneous power $P = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{v} = 0$ and work $W = \int dW = 0$ identically across *any* arc.

B.diagnostic: Confuses absence of atmospheric friction with the mathematical orthogonality of gravitational force and displacement.

C.diagnostic: Falsely claims gravity only works in 1D vertical motion.

D.diagnostic: Assumes work is non-zero over partial arcs and cancels globally, failing to see that $dW = 0$ point-by-point everywhere in circular motion.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the angle between the radial gravitational force and the tangential displacement in a circular orbit?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: A circle's radius and its tangent line are perpendicular at every point; therefore, $\theta = 90.0^\circ$ everywhere.

progressive_hints.title: Geometric Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What does the scalar dot product evaluate to when the angle between two non-zero vectors is $90.0^\circ$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B} = |\vec{A}||\vec{B}|\cos(90^\circ) = 0$. Orthogonal vectors have zero scalar product.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Does this zero work condition depend on completing a full revolution?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: No! Because $dW = \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{s} = 0$ at *every single instant*, the work done over *any* arc—even a microscopic fraction of a degree—is identically zero.

reasoning_ladder.understand: W = \int_{C} \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{s} - General line integral definition of mechanical work along a path C.
reasoning_ladder.represent: \vec{F}_g = -\frac{G M m}{r^2}\,\hat{r},\quad d\vec{s} = r\,d\phi\,\hat{\phi} - Polar coordinate vector representation on circular orbit.
reasoning_ladder.connect: \hat{r} \cdot \hat{\phi} = 0 \implies \vec{F}_g \cdot d\vec{s} = 0 - Orthogonality of radial and azimuthal basis vectors in Euclidean plane.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: dW = \vec{F}_g \cdot d\vec{s} = 0 \implies W = \int_{\phi_1}^{\phi_2} 0\,d\phi = 0\text{ for any } [\phi_1, \phi_2] - Vanishing integrand yields zero integral over any arbitrary domain.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: W = 0 \implies \Delta K = 0 \implies v = \text{const} - Work-energy theorem confirms speed remains invariant in uniform circular orbits.

derivation_steps: Step 1 (Understand the physical regime): W = \int_{C} \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{s} [General line integral definition of mechanical work along a path C.]
Step 2 (Represent the physical configuration): \vec{F}_g = -\frac{G M m}{r^2}\,\hat{r},\quad d\vec{s} = r\,d\phi\,\hat{\phi} [Polar coordinate vector representation on circular orbit.]
Step 3 (Connect governing physical laws): \hat{r} \cdot \hat{\phi} = 0 \implies \vec{F}_g \cdot d\vec{s} = 0 [Orthogonality of radial and azimuthal basis vectors in Euclidean plane.]

Step 4 (Calculate & execute formal derivation): dW = \vec{F}_g \cdot d\vec{s} = 0 \implies W = \int_{\phi_1}^{\phi_2} 0\,d\phi = 0\text{ for any } [\phi_1, \phi_2] [Vanishing integrand yields zero integral over any arbitrary domain.]
Step 5 (Interpret the physical outcome): W = 0 \implies \Delta K = 0 \implies v = \text{const} [Work-energy theorem confirms speed remains invariant in uniform circular orbits.]

limiting_cases.expected: F is not perpendicular to ds; gravity does work => W != 0 over partial arcs
All component projections and dependent vector products evaluate to 0.

questions.stem: A rigid horizontal lever arm of length $\vec{r} = 2.0\,\hat{i}\text{ m}$ lies along the positive $x$-axis pivoted at the origin. A force $\vec{F} = 15.0\,\hat{j}\text{ N}$ acts at its tip in the positive $y$-direction. Using the vector cross product definition of torque $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$, what is the torque vector and its rotational direction when viewed from the positive $z$-axis?

options.A: $\vec{\tau} = +30.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\;\hat{k}\text{ (out of the page, inducing counterclockwise rotation)}$
options.B: $\vec{\tau} = -30.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\;\hat{k}\text{ (into the page, inducing clockwise rotation)}$
options.D: $\vec{\tau} = 0.0\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\text{ because cross products vanish for perpendicular vectors}$

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Synthesize vector cross product determinant and assign orthogonal right-hand torque orientation.

A.diagnostic: Correct. $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F} = (2.0\hat{i}) \times (15.0\hat{j}) = 30.0(\hat{i} \times \hat{j}) = +30.0\hat{k}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$. By the right-hand rule, curling fingers from $+x$ into $+y$ points the thumb out of the page ($+z$), corresponding to counterclockwise rotation.

B.diagnostic: Computes $\vec{F} \times \vec{r} = -30.0\hat{k}$, failing to recognize that cross products are antisymmetric ($A \times B = -(B \times A)$).

C.diagnostic: Confuses torque units with Joules and directs torque parallel to the arm.

D.diagnostic: Confuses cross products with dot products; cross product is *maximized* when vectors are perpendicular.

progressive_hints.title: Decisive Physical Invariant
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the unit vector cross product $\hat{i} \times \hat{j}$ in a standard right-handed Cartesian coordinate system?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: In a right-handed system, $\hat{i} \times \hat{j} = +\hat{k}$ (pointing out of the page along the positive $z$-axis).

progressive_hints.title: Geometric Representation
progressive_hints.prompt_question: How do you evaluate $\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}$ with the given components?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $\vec{\tau} = (2.0\,\hat{i}) \times (15.0\,\hat{j}) = (2.0 \times 15.0)(\hat{i} \times \hat{j}) = +30.0\,\hat{k}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$.

progressive_hints.title: First Mathematical Pivot
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What physical rotational motion does a positive $z$-component ($+\hat{k}$) torque produce in the $xy$-plane?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: By convention of the right-hand grip rule, a torque vector pointing out of the page ($+\hat{k}$) produces counterclockwise rotational acceleration.

reasoning_ladder.understand: \vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F} - Axial pseudo-vector definition of rotational moment (torque).
